The equation separates, and the x-side turns out to be a standard eˣ(f + f′) integral.
**Step 1 — separate the variables.**
e^(−x)(y + 1) dy = −(cos²x − sin 2x) y dx
**(y + 1)/y dy = −eˣ(cos²x − sin 2x) dx**
**Step 2 — integrate the left side.**
∫(1 + 1/y) dy = **y + log y**
**Step 3 — integrate the right side.** Notice that
d/dx(cos²x) = 2 cos x(−sin x) = **−sin 2x**
so with f = cos²x we have f′ = −sin 2x, and the bracket is exactly **f + f′**. Using
∫eˣ(f + f′)dx = eˣ f:
∫eˣ(cos²x − sin 2x) dx = **eˣ cos²x**
and the right side, with its minus sign, integrates to −eˣcos²x.
**Step 4 — combine.**
y + log y = −eˣ cos²x + C
**y + log y + eˣ cos²x = C**
**Step 5 — use the initial condition** y = 1 when x = 0:
1 + log 1 + e⁰cos²0 = 1 + 0 + 1 = **2**, so C = 2
**y + log y + eˣ cos²x = 2** ✓
The recognition in step 3 is the whole difficulty; without it the integral ∫eˣcos²x dx needs
integration by parts twice. The appearance of **sin 2x** alongside **cos²x** is the signal,
since one is the derivative of the other.
∴ y + log y + eˣ cos²x = 2.
kcet|Mathematics|2016|20|MTG Karnataka-C:
**Order** is the order of the highest derivative present; **degree** is the power of that
derivative **once the equation has been made polynomial in all its derivatives**.
**Order.** The highest derivative appearing is **d²y/dx²**, so the order is **2** ✓ (all four
options agree on this).
**Degree.** The equation contains **sin(dy/dx)**. A sine cannot be cleared by raising the
equation to a power or rationalising it — expanding it as a series gives infinitely many
terms in dy/dx. The equation therefore **cannot be written as a polynomial** in the
derivatives, and the degree is **not defined** ✓ — option (d).
The fractional power 3/4 is a red herring: that alone could be removed by raising both
sides to the fourth power, giving
[1 + (dy/dx)² + sin(dy/dx)]³ = (d²y/dx²)⁴
But the sine survives that operation, so the obstruction remains.
The rule in general: **degree is undefined** whenever a derivative appears inside a
transcendental function — sin, cos, log, exponential — or in any way that cannot be reduced
to a whole-number power.
The companion question on the same page has [1 + (dy/dx)²]² = d²y/dx², with **no** sine. That
one **is** polynomial in its derivatives, so its degree is perfectly well defined, and the
contrast between the two is what both questions are testing.
∴ order = 2, degree = not defined.
kcet|Mathematics|2017|24|MTG Karnataka-C:
**Degree** is the power of the **highest-order** derivative, once the equation is polynomial
in all its derivatives.
**Step 1 — identify the highest-order derivative.** The equation contains dy/dx (order 1)
and d²y/dx² (order 2), so the highest order is **2** and the degree is the power of
**d²y/dx²**.
**Step 2 — check the equation is already polynomial.**
[1 + (dy/dx)²]² = d²y/dx²
There are no radicals, no fractional powers, and no derivative inside a sine or logarithm.
Both sides are polynomial in the derivatives ✓ so the degree is defined.
**Step 3 — read off the power of d²y/dx².** It appears to the first power:
**degree = 1** ✓
The trap is the visible **square** on the left, which tempts the answer 2 — option (c) — or
the 4 that would come from expanding [1 + (dy/dx)²]² and taking the highest power of dy/dx,
option (b). Neither is relevant: the degree is governed **only** by the highest-order
derivative, and the powers of lower-order ones do not count at all.
So, however complicated the dy/dx terms become, if d²y/dx² appears to the first power the
degree is 1.
This equation is in fact the one for the **radius of curvature** being constant, and it
describes a circle — which is why it appears so often.
∴ 1.
kcet|Mathematics|2019|30|MTG Karnataka-C:
The order of the differential equation obtained from a family of curves equals the number of
**independent** arbitrary constants — and here the four constants are not independent.
**Step 1 — simplify the expression.** Using e^(a+b) = e^a · e^b:
y = C₁ e^(C₂ + x) + C₃ e^(C₄ + x)
= C₁ e^(C₂) eˣ + C₃ e^(C₄) eˣ
**Step 2 — collect.** Both terms carry the same factor eˣ:
y = (C₁e^(C₂) + C₃e^(C₄)) eˣ
The bracket is a single constant; call it **A**:
**y = A eˣ**
**Step 3 — count.** The family contains just **one** arbitrary constant, so the differential
equation has order **1** ✓
**Step 4 — confirm by eliminating A.**
dy/dx = A eˣ = y
so the differential equation is **dy/dx = y** — manifestly first order, with no constants
left ✓
The question is a test of whether four letters are mistaken for four degrees of freedom.
They are not: C₂ and C₄ sit inside exponentials that factor out, and the products C₁e^(C₂)
and C₃e^(C₄) then merge into one. Four symbols, one genuine parameter.
The general principle: always **simplify the family first**, and count only the constants
that cannot be absorbed into one another.
∴ 1.

The substitution is signalled by the bracket, and the cosec x in the numerator turns out to
be exactly its derivative.
**Step 1 — substitute.** Let
u = 1 + log tan(x/2)
**Step 2 — differentiate u.** By the chain rule,
du/dx = (1/tan(x/2)) × sec²(x/2) × (1/2)
= 1/[2 sin(x/2) cos(x/2)]
and by the double-angle formula 2 sin(x/2)cos(x/2) = sin x, so
**du = dx/sin x = cosec x dx** ✓
The numerator is precisely du — which is why the integral is designed this way.
**Step 3 — rewrite the integral.**
∫ cosec x dx / cos²(1 + log tan(x/2)) = ∫ du/cos²u = ∫ **sec²u** du
**Step 4 — integrate.**
= tan u + c
= **tan[1 + log tan(x/2)] + c** ✓
**Check by differentiating:**
d/dx tan[1 + log tan(x/2)] = sec²[·] × cosec x = cosec x/cos²[·] ✓ the integrand
The identity **d/dx[log tan(x/2)] = cosec x** is worth knowing in its own right — it is the
standard antiderivative of cosec x, usually written ∫cosec x dx = log|tan(x/2)| + c, and
this question is that result used in reverse.
Option (c), sec², is the **integrand's** shape rather than the integral's; option (a) squares
the wrong function.
∴ tan[1 + log tan(x/2)] + c.
kcet|Mathematics|2016|47|MTG Karnataka-C:
The limits are **symmetric about zero**, so the only thing that matters is whether the
integrand is **odd** or **even**.
**Step 1 — test the parity of f(x) = sin¹⁰³x · cos¹⁰¹x.**
f(−x) = sin¹⁰³(−x) · cos¹⁰¹(−x)
Now sin(−x) = −sin x, raised to the **odd** power 103 gives **−sin¹⁰³x**
and cos(−x) = cos x, raised to any power gives **+cos¹⁰¹x**
So
f(−x) = (−sin¹⁰³x)(cos¹⁰¹x) = **−f(x)**
The integrand is **odd** ✓
**Step 2 — apply the symmetry rule.** For any odd function,
**∫₋ₐᵃ f(x) dx = 0**
because the signed area to the left of the origin exactly cancels that to the right.
Therefore
∫₋π/4^(π/4) sin¹⁰³x cos¹⁰¹x dx = **0** ✓
The huge exponents are pure decoration — no antiderivative is needed, and none would be
practicable. All that matters is that **103 is odd**, which makes the whole product odd.
The rule to carry away: a product of sines and cosines is **odd** exactly when the total
power of **sine** is odd, since cosine contributes no sign change. Had the sine exponent
been even, the integrand would have been even and the integral non-zero — and then the
exponents really would have mattered.
∴ 0.
